title: Non-singlets and the phase diagram of Matrix Quantum Mechanics
authors: Igor R. Klebanov, Henry W. Lin, Pavel Meshcheriakov, Jessica Yeh
abstract: The quantum mechanics of one $N\times N$ Hermitian matrix in the infinite $N$ limit is well known to define a two-dimensional string theory when the quartic coupling constant $g$ is tuned to a special negative value $g_*$. We study the thermodynamics of this Matrix Quantum Mechanics (MQM), treating the SU$(N)$ symmetry as a global symmetry. Crucially, the non-singlets, i.e. states in non-trivial representations of SU$(N)$, implement the effects of vortices on the discretized worldsheets. This random lattice model has the low-temperature $c=1$ and high-temperature $c=0$ phases, with the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) transition separating them. We map out the phase diagram in the coupling--temperature plane, which is separated by the critical stability curve $T_c(g)$ extending from $g_*< g <0$. We study this curve using the non-perturbative matrix bootstrap and low- and high-temperature perturbation theory, which explain the thermal instability. At low temperatures, thermally excited non-singlets backreact on the Fermi sea of matrix eigenvalues, causing it to spill over. At high temperatures, the theory is described by an effective matrix integral obtained by dimensional reduction on the thermal circle; the eigenvalue distribution of the zero mode becomes unstable at the critical coupling. We conjecture that the BKT transition occurs at a special point on the critical curve and estimate its position. Finally, we switch to the regular square lattice and study the MQM-inspired Villain model, where the link factor is the one-dimensional propagator on a circle. Using Monte Carlo simulations, we map out the BKT transition in this model.
summary: This work analyzes the thermal phase diagram of Matrix Quantum Mechanics, a model relevant to string theory, by studying the interplay between singlet and non-singlet states. The authors map out the phase boundary, predicting a BKT transition separating different critical phases. The methodology combines advanced analytical techniques with numerical simulations to characterize this complex phase structure.
main_problem: The paper investigates the thermodynamics and phase diagram of Matrix Quantum Mechanics (MQM) in the infinite N limit, focusing on the role of non-singlet states.
main_result: The authors map out the phase diagram in the coupling-temperature plane, identifying a Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) transition separating low-temperature (c=1) and high-temperature (c=0) phases.
method: The study employs analytical techniques like non-perturbative matrix bootstrap and perturbation theory, supplemented by Monte Carlo simulations on an inspired lattice model.
model_or_system: The system is the quantum mechanics of an N x N Hermitian matrix with a quartic potential, analyzed in the large N limit. The model exhibits distinct singlet and non-singlet sectors.
key_observables: The critical stability curve T_c(g), the BKT transition temperature T_BKT, and the eigenvalue distribution of the zero mode.
important_parameters: The coupling constant g, the temperature T, and the large N limit.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on treating the SU(N) symmetry as a global symmetry and utilizing the large N limit to connect to string theory.
figures_summary: The notes mention Figure 1 showing the thermal phase diagram and Figure 2 illustrating three scenarios for the BKT transition location on the critical curve.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first analyzing the large N limit and the role of non-singlets, deriving the critical curve T_c(g) using various theoretical tools, and finally extending the study to a regular square lattice using a Villain model analyzed via Monte Carlo simulations.
why_interesting: The study of phase transitions (like BKT) in complex, interacting quantum systems, even those derived from matrix models, provides deep insights into critical phenomena relevant to many-body physics and condensed matter systems.

In scenario II, the critical curve Tc(g) remains analytic down to g∗. Since the high-temperature branch corresponds to c = 0 gravity, the entire finite-temperature critical curve would belong to the c = 0 universality class, while the c = 1 theory is reached only at zero temperature. This scenario may therefore be interpreted as a zero-temperature BKT transition.
